text: We can move the deletion of existing Pods to a dedicated controller (or even to ). However, workload controllers still must obey the rule: when has , stop Pod creation and wait until is gone. If the controller that creates Pods does not pause while victim Pods terminate, it immediately creates replacement Pods. Then the controller and the workload controller fight each other in a loop (one creates Pods while the other deletes them). This loop also keeps the finalizer on and blocks deletion. A dedicated controller reduces the responsibility of workload controllers, but it does not remove the fragile contract around pausing Pod creation and controller delegation.

text: Thanks for looking! Nobody starts the interactive REPL on purpose with stdin set to NUL. The trouble is that tools which run commands non-interactively hand the process NUL as stdin, and since NUL is a character device, reports True. So an accidental bare , or with an empty heredoc, lands in pyrepl instead of reading EOF and exiting. Where I hit it: AI coding agents. Claude Code's shell tool on Windows runs every command with stdin = NUL and output captured, so anyone using it on Windows can hit this. The process never returns: it spins writing tracebacks (about 4 MB in 3 seconds here) until the tool's timeout kills it. hyperfine also defaults stdin to NUL (that's how #133430 got there), and CI runners and schedulers commonly do the same. The basic REPL ( ) reads EOF and exits at once, which is what these tools need. A possible check: fails on NUL even though succeeds: So pyrepl could fall back to the basic REPL when fails on stdin, or at least stop retrying after the first from .

text: **Update / root cause on my side (follow-up to my earlier comments):** In my case this turned out **not** to be a bug in the integration or in – the entity had been **disabled in the entity registry**. A disabled entity is never added to hass, so it never subscribes to the dispatcher signal and therefore never fires . After re-enabling the entity and restarting Home Assistant, everything works again on 2026.10.1. To verify, I ran a copy of the core integration (unchanged apart from added log lines) as a custom component and traced the full path. Before the fix: …and nothing else – no entity was listening. After re-enabling the entity: **Important for others landing here:** the debug line is **not** the cause of missing events. The integration uses the library's raw ERP1 callback ( ), which is emitted *before* EEP decoding. text: One reservation I have from the build backend side of things is that it's not fully clear to me how to wire this up while at the same time allowing users to choose. My understanding from the PEP is that this is "just" about ensuring that globally distributed binaries (Linux distro packages, conda, cibuildwheel outputs published to PyPI, etc.) don't hinder adoption for users that need to do tracing. text: Thanks @user. [PEP 831](http enables frame pointers by default in CPython and strongly recommends the same throughout Python's native ecosystem, including extensions and their dependencies. The recommendation also covers local builds. Each build system and project needs to work out how to implement it across its builds; the PEP cannot prescribe that for every setup. We expect this to take time, and that's fine. The goal remains frame pointers throughout the native ecosystem. Your static-library example is a real limitation. The setting needs to reach those libraries and subprojects when they are compiled, since adding flags only to the bindings leaves gaps in stack unwinding. Dependencies supplied as binaries would need to be rebuilt by whoever distributes them. There are examples to follow. [Ubuntu](http and [Fedora](http already adopted frame-pointer defaults. Ubuntu originally exempted Python; upstream CPython 3.15 now enables them. [python-build-standalone's change](http adds them to shared target flags, which dependency builds such as [SQLite](http also consume. Ideally, manylinux and other dependency-build pipelines would apply this to the libraries they build too. That will require coordination and rebuilding over time. For Meson, would a build-wide setting that reaches subprojects be workable? This PR is intended to make the relevant information available to backends, while projects work through how to apply it to their dependencies.

text: I have reproduced a hang in both and on an M1 Mac by dropping a single client UDP datagram in a temporary diagnostic build. Both get stuck in . Sampling the process showed it waiting in through the blocking QUIC read path. The client is explicitly nonblocking, while the accepted server connection inherits blocking mode from the listener. I checked this at runtime: returned 0 for the client and 1 for the server. The underlying UDP sockets are nonblocking in both cases. In these two scripts, the same interpreter thread drives both endpoints and advances the simulated clock. A blocking continues to service the server's QUIC events, but the interpreter can't run the client to retransmit the lost data. The simulated clock also stops advancing. The interpreter own 60 second deadline can't interrupt that call. Making the accepted server connection nonblocking lets both scripts recover from the dropped datagram and finish. All 114 RADIX scripts also passed with that experimental change. To check whether this was hiding a problem in blocking reads, I kept the server blocking and added a temporary worker to tick the client and advance the simulated clock during the read. Both scripts recovered and completed with still returning 1 for the server. Ticking the client alone still hung, as did advancing the clock alone. This points to a RADIX execution problem. RADIX deliberately enables for its blocking tests, including . We should keep that support and make blocking mode an explicit choice for tests that provide independent progress. I will work on a PR for this.

text: Quick update here. We've been working on figuring out the cause of the task failures and have made some progress in the past few months. The RAM itself should be fine, as it passed every single test. Since the SIGILL issue can be observed on both builders (mipsle and mips64le) and even in kernel space (see http we decided to dive into it first. We deployed a BadInstr (a register in CP0) check in the reserved instruction (RI) exception handler, and found it somehow mismatched the instruction read from RAM every time we saw a task failure caused by SIGILL. In this failure pattern, the decoder sees an illegal instruction and traps into an RI exception, with BadInstr containing what it has seen. The instruction located in RAM is still legal. This hints that the instruction cache and the data cache behave differently in some edge cases! The illegal instruction in BadInstr, however, is never similar to the legal one in RAM. We haven't seen any cache error either (all cache levels have internal ECC). Thus, it's not a bitflip issue. Next, we deployed a hack to the BadInstr check to verify our theory. The hack flushes the instruction cache by calling and returns to userspace to resume execution. Guess what, the execution finishes without trapping into another RI exception. Task failures caused by SIGILL are gone since then! So it seems SIGSEGV is just another failure pattern where the mismatched instruction in the instruction cache happens to be legal. The same failure pattern also has the potential to cause other categories of test failures. Currently, we are still working on figuring out the root cause and hopefully fixing or working around it. We suspect a kernel bug (faulty context switch?) or an undiscovered CPU errata.

text: I need to correct my own analysis in the issue description — it was wrong, and I apologise for the noise. UnicodeEncodeError.start / .end are indices into exc.object, which for BufferedIncrementalEncoder is the concatenation self.buffer + input (the str that _buffer_encode receives), not a byte offset. For the reproducer: enc = codecs.getincrementalencoder("idna")() enc.encode("é") # held in the buffer enc.encode("." + "a"*64, True) exc.object is "é." + "a"*64 (66 characters). "a"*64 starts at index 2 of that string, so start=2, end=66 is correct. I confused the byte length of the punycode-encoded label (b"xn--9ca", 7 bytes) with the character length of the label inside exc.object ("é", 1 character). len(encoded) is not comparable to the str index that start/end refer to. The existing code (size += len(label)) is correct. My suggested change (size += len(encoded)) would produce start=8, end=72, which is wrong: end=72 exceeds len(exc.object)=66. So there is no bug in Lib/encodings/idna.py. I'm closing this issue as not-a-bug. @user — sorry for sending you down this path. The PR #159233 should be closed; there is nothing to fix here. text: I have opened #33213. The packet loss filter from my earlier probe isn't needed to trigger the hang. After a key update, OpenSSL retains the previous receive keys for one probe timeout (PTO). If the client starts another update while the server still retains those keys, the server discards its packets, as allowed by [RFC 9001 section 6.5](http The peers can have very different PTOs. RADIX advances its fake clock by 1 ms per interpreter step, so extra handshake retries can inflate the initial RTT estimate. During the data loop, the server's estimate can stay high while the client gets shorter samples. The client waits three of its own PTOs after confirmation of the previous update, but the server can still be retaining its old keys when the next update arrives. The blocking server read then stops the interpreter, which also needs to drive the client's retransmission. It can't advance the fake clock while it's inside either, so recovery gets stuck. The two SIGABRT jobs look like the same hang. At their source revisions, the scripts following the last completed iterations are these same key update tests, and the elapsed time matches the watchdog calling after 1800 seconds. The PR makes clients and listeners nonblocking when RADIX creates them, and accepted connections inherit that setting. Waiting reads can return control to the interpreter, while stays enabled for tests that need blocking . The regression delays an ACK to give the server a larger PTO, then exercises successive client key updates. The old setup hangs with the mode checks removed; with the fix, it recovers without a packet loss filter. I have checked the full RADIX suite on my M1 with threads and without them, keeping the usual skips in the latter build. The new test also passed 150 repetitions, with qlog enabled for half of those runs.
